subject: armadillo
pitch: A nine-banded armadillo trotting along. A shell of overlapping banded plates in dusty pinkish-tan, a pointy snout, tall leathery ears, small beady eyes, sturdy clawed feet and a long armoured tail tapering to a point. A sprinkle of coarse pale hairs pokes out between the bands.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the armadillo's proportions and rest pose, then planning the skeleton structure — hips as root, with spine, head, tail, and leg chains branching off.

Now I'm working out the body geometry using a swept ellipse profile along the spine curve, and laying out exact joint coordinates for the spine chain and the neck/head chain with their parent relationships.

I'm defining the head's parts — orienting the head joint along the forward tangent, then adding the skull sphere and a cone-shaped snout positioned and angled off the head's local forward/up axes.

Now I'm adding the jaw as a child joint of the head with its own small thin cone part, then working out the ears using a flattened extrusion with an outline shape standing upright on top of the head, oriented sideways to face outward.

Next I'm placing the eyes as small dark spheres positioned on the head's surface, offset sideways and slightly up, sized to roughly match the skull sphere radius.

Then I'm working out the snout length and head joint placement so the cone fits proportionally with the armadillo's overall body length, adding a small dark nose sphere at the tip.

For the shell, I'm planning the carapace as scapular and pelvic shields with nine bands between them, considering a lathe-based approach around the spine axis to build each ring segment.

Trying a partial cylinder ring scaled elliptically over the top arc for each band, but weighing whether torus segments lying in the XY plane with a rotated axis would better capture the dome shape covering the back and sides while leaving the belly open.

Still building the band layout...

I realize naively scaling a torus geometry would squash the tube thickness unevenly between the z-direction and radial direction, so I need to construct each band's geometry directly with the right radius and tube values rather than scaling a unit torus.

For the torus geometry, I'll use the radial dimension as the base radius, a small tube thickness, then scale the y-axis by the ratio of the two radii to get the right proportions with flat shading. For coloring I'll keep it simple with alternating plate tones and a darker edge color rather than gradients.

Instead of heavy scute or stud geometry, I'll skip those and focus on adding sparse hair-like spikes poking out at the band boundaries on the sides of the body, using pale-colored thin rods placed at specific angles to suggest fur peeking from under the shell.

Now I'm setting up the four legs with simple IK chains — short sturdy hind legs with hip, knee, and ankle joints positioned to keep the armadillo's stance low and compact, bending knees forward like a real armadillo's hind limbs.

I'm parenting hind legs to the base of the spine and front legs further up, tagging them as "leg" role with ground contact points, then sweeping a tapered cylinder along each chain in skin-tone color to build the leg geometry.

Now I'm adding feet: a small box pad at the ankle joint, plus two or three cone-shaped claws angled forward and downward, with front claws made slightly longer than hind ones.

Next I'm setting up the tail chain as a sequence of points curving down and back from the hips, using a catmull-rom spline parented off the spine joint for smooth bending.

Building tail ring geometry...

Writing sweep radius logic...

Now I'm placing the hips root joint and spine chain with catmull-rom path segments, then moving to the head: a scaled skull sphere plus a snout cone with its base and tip positions defined along the forward axis.

Working out the jaw joint position and aim direction, sizing a lower jaw cone with its own radius and length, and noting the overlap concern with the upper snout cone.

Now adding head detailing: a tan skin tone for the base and a plated shield cap on the crown using a partial sphere geometry, scaled to fit the skull shape. Then I'm starting to place the ears behind and lateral to the head with a thin extruded shape.

Tilting the ear back and setting its thickness so the inner face sits just forward of the outer surface. Positioning dark eye spheres near the skull surface using the head-local offsets, and considering a tiny white highlight sphere for shine. Starting to think through hair spike placement next.

Now laying out the tail ring geometry: nine mid-body bands plus four scapular shield bands up front and five pelvic shield bands toward the back, spacing them along the z-axis at regular intervals.

I'm sizing the tube radii for the shield versus mid rings so they overlap slightly, alternating colors between the two plate shades for texture, and adding small squashed-sphere studs scattered around each shield band for a scute-like detail.

Still working out torus geometry...

Adjusting proportions further, lowering the body center and rechecking leg bend angles so it reads as cartoonish but balanced, then moving on to planning the hair spikes along the spine bands.

Writing spike placement code...

For the bone mapping, I'm defining spine joint ranges by z-position so each hair/spike picks the nearest bone segment to attach to, with separate logic for the head and neck region.

I'm setting up the leg rigs now, naming the chains per limb (hip/knee/ankle for hind legs, shoulder/elbow/wrist for front) and sweeping each leg with a tapering skin-colored radius down to a rounded tip. Tail rings get chained off the first spine joint, with the tail path starting near the hips.

I'm placing the tail control points so they curve gently down toward the ground without clipping below the feet, then mapping the body sweep radius as a function of the spine path's parameter t.

Working out the elliptical falloff for the belly and shell bands, making sure the belly radius tapers to zero at the ends while the shell extends slightly further out near the tail opening.

Still writing torus geometry...

I check the cross product of the ear's tilt vectors to confirm the thickness direction points mostly forward, which looks right. That settles it, so I'll finalize and write out the code.
